context: Current closing price of L3Harris (LHX): $278.92 USD as of 2026-07-31.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent price near $279, with very little directional conviction. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing level since overnight moves in most liquid assets tend to be small relative to longer-run variation, and I had no strong catalyst information to justify a large departure. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $280, reflecting a mild assumption of positive drift that is common in equity or commodity markets over short windows, but essentially treating the near-term outlook as roughly flat. At the one-month horizon, I moved the point estimate to $282, again reflecting a small positive drift assumption rather than any specific fundamental view — essentially extrapolating a gentle trend while acknowledging that a month is long enough for meaningful mean-reversion or trend continuation to play out.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect typical realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, the $6 half-width on either side of the estimate corresponds to a relatively tight range consistent with daily price fluctuations in a moderately volatile asset. At one week, I widened the interval to $12 on each side, roughly reflecting the compounding of daily uncertainty over five trading sessions. At one month, the interval spans $24 on each side, acknowledging that over roughly 20 trading days, accumulated uncertainty grows substantially and a wide range of outcomes becomes plausible even without any specific adverse scenario in mind.

Several risks could push outcomes well outside these intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as stronger-than-expected economic data, a policy announcement, or a sector-specific development — could produce a sharp rally that breaks through the upper bound, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. On the downside, macroeconomic shocks, geopolitical escalation, or a broad risk-off episode could drive prices sharply below the lower bounds. My intervals implicitly assume relatively normal market conditions, so fat-tail events — the kind that occur a few times per decade but can move prices 10–20% in days — are underweighted in the stated ranges. Liquidity crunches or correlated selling across asset classes represent the most serious tail risks that could invalidate the intervals entirely.
